overview:
Equatorial Guinea is one of the smallest countries on mainland Africa, about the size of Maryland, and it comes in two parts. Río Muni is a rectangle of rainforest on the coast of Central Africa between Cameroon and Gabon. The island of Bioko lies 40 kilometers off Cameroon's shore in the Gulf of Guinea, and it is there, not on the mainland, that the capital, Malabo, sits beneath a mist-wrapped volcano. Several smaller islands, including distant Annobón, complete the country.

About 1.7 million people live in Equatorial Guinea. Spanish is the main official language, a legacy of Spanish rule, making this the only Spanish-speaking country in Africa; French and Portuguese are also official, and Fang and Bubi are widely spoken at home. Oil discovered offshore in the 1990s made the country one of the richest in Africa by average income, and it built a brand-new planned city called Ciudad de la Paz in the forest. Yet the wealth is shared very unequally, and the same president has ruled since 1979, one of the longest reigns of any leader in the world.
landAndNature: Bioko island is a chain of volcanoes; Pico Basilé rises 3,011 meters directly above Malabo, and its southern slopes are among the wettest places in Africa, with more than 10 meters of rain a year. Those rainforests shelter seven kinds of monkeys, including the drill, and beaches where four species of sea turtle come ashore to nest. Río Muni on the mainland is low coastal plain climbing to forested hills, drained by rivers such as the Mbini. Monte Alén National Park protects lowland gorillas, chimpanzees, forest elephants, and the goliath frog, the largest frog in the world. Annobón, far to the southwest, is a tiny green volcanic island with a crater lake. The climate is hot and humid year-round.
peopleAndCulture: The Fang are the largest people on the mainland, while the Bubi are the original inhabitants of Bioko, and small communities of Fernandinos, descended from freed slaves, and Annobonese have their own Portuguese-based creole. Most people are Roman Catholic. Meals are built on cassava, plantains, and yams with fish or meat in peanut or palm-nut sauce, and pepper soup, a fiery broth with fish, is a favorite. Fang storytellers perform epic tales accompanied by the mvet, a harp-zither with a gourd resonator, and the balélé dance is performed on Bioko at Christmas. Soccer is the favorite sport; the country hosted the Africa Cup of Nations in 2012 and 2015, and the women's team has won the African championship twice.
history: Pygmy peoples and then Bubi and Fang settlers lived here before Portuguese sailors reached Bioko in 1472. Portugal traded the islands to Spain in 1778, and Spain slowly extended control to the mainland in the late 1800s, running cocoa plantations on Bioko with imported labor. Independence came on October 12, 1968, under Francisco Macías Nguema, whose rule became one of the most brutal in Africa; roughly a third of the population fled or died. His nephew Teodoro Obiang overthrew him in 1979 and has been president ever since. Oil production from 1996 brought sudden wealth, new highways, and towering government buildings, but human rights groups criticize the lack of political freedom and the poverty in which most citizens still live.
funFacts: Equatorial Guinea is the only country in Africa where Spanish is an official language.
Despite its name, the equator does not pass through Equatorial Guinea; the island of Annobón lies just south of it.
The goliath frog of Río Muni can weigh over three kilograms and grow longer than a house cat.
The capital, Malabo, is on an island, while a brand-new capital called Ciudad de la Paz is being built on the mainland.
The country's oil made its average income among the highest in Africa, but most of the money reaches only a few.
